text: Solomon made a marriage alliance with Pharaoh king of Egypt. He took Pharaoh's daughter and brought her to the City of David until he had finished building his own house, the house of the LORD, and the wall around Jerusalem.
The people, however, were still sacrificing at the high places, because no house had yet been built for the name of the LORD.
Solomon loved the LORD, walking in the statutes of his father David—except that he sacrificed and burned incense at the high places.
The king went to Gibeon to sacrifice there, for that was the great high place; Solomon offered a thousand burnt offerings on that altar.
At Gibeon the LORD appeared to Solomon in a dream by night, and God said, "Ask what I should give you."

Solomon answered, "You showed great kindness to your servant David, my father, because he walked before you in faithfulness and righteousness and uprightness of heart toward you. You have kept for him this great kindness and have given him a son to sit on his throne this very day.
And now, LORD my God, you have made your servant king in place of my father David, but I am only a young man; I do not know how to go out or come in.
Your servant is among your people whom you have chosen, a people so numerous they cannot be counted or numbered.
So give your servant a listening heart to judge your people, to discern between good and evil—for who is able to judge this great people of yours?"
It pleased the LORD that Solomon had asked for this.

versions.text: It pleased the Lord that Solomon had asked for this.
versions.explanation: The divine name is rendered "the LORD" elsewhere in the chapter (vv. 1–7) but "the Lord" here and in verse 15, creating an inconsistency in the printed text; unify the form unless the distinction is deliberate.

text: God said to him, "Because you have asked for this and have not asked for long life for yourself, or riches, or the death of your enemies, but have asked for discernment to hear a case rightly,
I now do as you have asked. I give you a heart so wise and discerning that no one like you has ever lived before you, and no one like you will arise after you.

versions.text: I now do as you have asked. I give you a wise and understanding heart, so that there has been no one like you before you, and none like you shall arise after you.
versions.explanation: The result clause "so that there has been no one like you before you" is grammatically awkward, since a present gift cannot cause a past state. Recasting the relative clause keeps the sense of אֲשֶׁר and reads more smoothly aloud.

text: I also give you what you did not ask for: both riches and honor, so that among kings there will be no one like you all your days.
And if you walk in my ways, keeping my statutes and my commandments, as your father David walked, I will lengthen your days."

Then Solomon awoke—and it had been a dream. He went to Jerusalem, stood before the ark of the covenant of the Lord, offered burnt offerings and fellowship offerings, and gave a banquet for all his servants.
Then two women who were prostitutes came to the king and stood before him.
One of the women said, "Please, my lord, this woman and I live in the same house, and I gave birth while she was there in the house.
On the third day after I gave birth, this woman also had a child. We were alone; there was no stranger with us in the house—only the two of us.
During the night this woman's son died, because she lay on him.
So she got up in the middle of the night and took my son from beside me while your servant was asleep. She laid him at her breast and laid her dead son at mine.
When I got up in the morning to nurse my son, there he was—dead. But when I looked at him closely in the morning, I saw that he was not the son I had borne."

versions.text: When I got up in the morning to nurse my son, there he was—dead. But when I looked at him closely in the morning light, I saw it was not the son I had borne."
versions.explanation: "Morning light" adds a detail not in the Hebrew (בַּבֹּקֶר, simply "in the morning"); the repetition of "in the morning" is present in the source and is natural in oral reading.

text: The other woman said, "No! The living one is my son; the dead one is yours." But the first insisted, "No! The dead one is yours; the living one is mine." So they argued before the king.
Then the king said, "One says, 'This is my son who is alive, and your son is dead,' and the other says, 'No! Your son is dead, and my son is alive.'"
So the king said, "Bring me a sword." And they brought a sword before the king.
Then the king ordered, "Cut the living child in two, and give half to one and half to the other."

But the woman whose son was alive was moved with deep compassion for her son and said to the king, "Please, my lord, give her the living child—only do not kill him!" The other said, "He shall be neither mine nor yours. Cut him in two!"
Then the king gave his ruling: "Give the living child to her; do not kill him. She is his mother."

versions.text: Then the king gave his ruling: "Give the living child to the first woman; do not kill him. She is his mother."
versions.explanation: The Hebrew has only the pronoun לָהּ ("to her"), referring to the woman who had just pleaded. "The first woman" is an interpretive addition that can confuse listeners, since "the first" was used differently in verse 22.

text: When all Israel heard the verdict the king had given, they stood in awe of him, for they saw that the wisdom of God was in him to administer justice.
